newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian markets ready for Yeltsin operation.
newsitem.headline: Russian markets ready for Yeltsin operation.

text.p: Russian financial markets are readying for President Boris Yeltsin's heart operation, but whether he lives or dies, dealers said on Monday that Russia's economic problems would be a more important influence on prices.
If Yeltsin dies, traders agree that prices on all markets will fall. But forecasts range from a short sharp drop to complete collapse and crash.
If the operation, expected in the next few days, restores Yeltsin to full activity, the euphoria will quickly fade as attention turns again to the intractable budget crisis.
"If Yeltsin is all right, it will be good for all the markets," said United City Bank chief currency dealer Alexander Suchkov.
"But the 1997 budget will be the main economic factor. Yeltsin, even in good shape, does not decide everything. The question is how the government will handle it."
Russian share prices, which went from record lows earlier this year to record highs on July 4 after Yeltsin was re-elected, have been the most sensitive to news about his health.
Equities dealers are betting on Yeltsin coming through, and are still buying in the hope of a five to seven percent rise in prices.
"It's 99.9 percent sure -- the first reaction will be to raise prices," said Regent European Securities senior trader Dmitry Starenko. "After the operation there will be one political risk less."

But whether an initial jump in prices on news that Yeltsin had survived would translate into a sustained rally depended on whether Western investors take the news as a signal at long last to pour funds into Russia, dealers said.
A failed operation would lead to bout of sharp selling which could turn into a rout, they said.
The rouble rarely reacts to political news, as it is strictly controlled by the central bank. But dealers said the death of Yeltsin would cause a limited fall in the currency.
"Nothing dramatic will happen to the rouble even if the result of the operation is the most unfavourable," Suchkov said.
The rouble eased on Monday, falling to a late 5,464/66 per dollar from 5,461/63 late on Friday.
Dealers said investors may have been taking funds out of government bonds as a precaution ahead of the operation, increasing the supply of roubles on the market.

Yeltsin's death would mean a new election should be called within three months. But an election campaign would make it harder for the government to collect unpaid taxes and undertake other unpopular measures needed to restore financial health.
"Banks would shift their investments out of government bonds and into dollars. But a big rouble fall is not likely," said Inkombank dealer Dzhamil Asfari.
Treasury bill dealers said the death of Yeltsin would push up Treasury bill yields to 60 percent from around 50 percent.
But if he survives, the government's budget operations would limit the fall in yields to about 45 percent.
"Even if the Yeltsin factor goes, the budget issue still remains a serious problem," said Dmitry Falkovich, fixed-income trader and analyst at Alliance Menatep.

The government collected only 74 percent of budgeted revenues in the first nine months of this year, and the International Monetary Fund last month delayed payment of the next tranche of its $10 billion loan to Russia because of worries about its poor tax performance.

Dealers said the very shortest paper would be safe whatever happens. Under the constitution, if Yeltsin dies or is incapacitated, he would be replaced by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin for three months to prepare for new elections.

"As an investor, Russia, no matter what happens with Yeltsin, is good for three months," he said. "If I put my money into three-month T-bills they will be repaid," said Nicholas Jordan, head of capital markets at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
